title: Ethics: virtue, duty, consequences, natural law
note: Normative theories answer what makes actions right. Consequentialists look to outcomes, deontologists to duties and rights, virtue ethicists to character, and natural law theorists to the goods of human nature known by reason. Metaethics asks what moral claims are and whether they can be objectively true.

read.title: Four ways to ask what is right
text: Imagine you could save five patients by secretly taking the organs of one healthy visitor. Different moral theories explain differently why most people recoil.

A consequentialist judges acts by their results. Classical utilitarians such as Bentham and Mill hold that the right act produces the greatest balance of happiness over suffering for everyone affected. A careful utilitarian may reply that a practice of secret killings would spread fear and destroy trust in hospitals, so the long-run results are terrible.
A deontologist says some acts are wrong whatever the results. For Kant, killing the visitor uses a person merely as a means and violates his dignity.
A virtue ethicist asks what a just and compassionate person would do. Such a person would not even treat the option as live, because practical wisdom sees that this is murder.

A natural law theorist, following Aquinas, holds that human life is a basic good that reason recognizes. One may never intentionally destroy it, even to bring about other goods, although one may sometimes accept a harm that is foreseen but not intended.
Each theory captures something real. Studying them helps us see which features of an action matter and why.
